notes.meaning: Sanballat grew extremely angry when he learned that the Jews were rebuilding the city wall. Instead of ignoring them, he mocked the builders and tried to make their efforts look foolish. Those who oppose God often use insults when they realize they cannot stop His work.

Sanballat publicly ridiculed the workers in front of his officials and the army of Samaria. He questioned their ability to finish the job and mocked them for using crumbling, burned stones. He did not believe God would step in to give such a small, weak group success.

Tobiah joined in the mockery by joking that even a light fox climbing on the wall would knock it down. He wanted to make the Jewish construction look weak and useless. People who want to stop good work often band together to discourage the workers.

Rather than trading insults with his enemies, Nehemiah took his pain straight to God in prayer. He asked the Lord to turn their insults back on them and punish them for trying to crush the builders. He left the outcome in God's hands because the enemies had really insulted God Himself.

differ.view: Christians should not copy this prayer for harm, because Jesus commands His followers to love and pray for their persecutors.
This prayer is acceptable because it was not personal revenge, but a righteous appeal for God to uphold His glory against sworn enemies.

notes.meaning: The Jews kept working without stopping and built the entire wall to half its intended height. The work moved forward quickly because the people threw their whole hearts into the task. When people are united in purpose, God helps them make great progress despite criticism.

Surrounding enemies on every side became furious when they saw the gaps in the wall closing up. They formed a plot to march against Jerusalem together to attack the city and stop the construction. God's enemies often set aside their own differences to oppose His plans.

The Jews responded to the threat by praying to God and setting up armed guards day and night. Nehemiah combined complete trust in God with practical actions for defense. True faith leads believers both to seek God's help and to remain watchful.

The people of Judah began to lose heart because the heavy physical labor was wearing them out. Massive piles of broken stone and dirt still had to be cleared before the wall could be finished. Hard work and constant tension can wear down even dedicated workers.

The enemies plotted a sudden, secret raid to kill the workers before anyone noticed them coming. They believed that killing the builders was the surest way to stop the work permanently. The threat of violence was aimed at crushing the builders' morale.

Jews living in nearby rural areas repeatedly came to Jerusalem to warn the builders about the plots against them. They feared that the attackers would strike from every direction while the men were away from home. God used these reports to expose the enemy's secret plans before they could happen.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest a slight change in the Hebrew text so the verse reads that the neighbors reported what the enemies were plotting against them.

notes.meaning: Nehemiah placed armed guards in the lowest, most exposed spots along the wall where an attack was most likely. He arranged the defenders by family groups, armed with swords, spears, and bows. Fighting alongside their own families gave each person a stronger reason to stand firm.

Nehemiah inspected the lines and urged the leaders and people not to be terrified. He reminded them that the Lord is far greater and more fearsome than any enemy army. He challenged them to fight bravely for their wives, children, and homes.

When the enemies realized their secret plan had been discovered, they backed off and gave up their attack. Nehemiah credited God with wrecking their scheme. With the crisis past, every worker returned to his post on the wall.

From that day forward, Nehemiah divided his personal workforce into two groups. Half of them continued the physical building, while the other half stood ready in full armor holding spears, shields, and bows. The community leaders stood right behind the workers to direct and encourage them.

The laborers hauling materials adapted their work so they could protect themselves at a moment's notice. They carried loads with one hand while holding a weapon ready with the other. This readiness showed that building and defending had to go hand in hand.

The stone masons needed both hands for their craft, so each man worked with a sword strapped directly to his side. Nehemiah kept a trumpeter right next to him so he could sound an instant alarm if an attack began. Being constantly prepared kept the builders safe without halting the work.

Nehemiah reminded the leaders and people that the wall was enormous and the workers were scattered far apart. He told them to rush toward the trumpet sound whenever they heard it blow. He assured them that God Himself would fight on their behalf.

The people worked relentlessly from the earliest light of dawn until the evening stars appeared in the sky. During all those hours, half the men stood guard holding their spears to prevent a surprise raid. Their persistent effort kept the work moving steadily forward.

Nehemiah ordered the workers and their helpers who lived in outlying villages to sleep inside Jerusalem instead of going home. This kept the workforce close together so they could serve as guards by night and build by day. Having everyone stay inside the walls strengthened the defenses of the whole city.

Nehemiah, his relatives, his servants, and his guards remained in constant readiness day and night. None of them took off their clothes to sleep, keeping their weapons within reach at all times. Their dedication set a powerful example of vigilance for the entire community.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Latin Vulgate translates the end of this verse to say that the men only took off their garments to bathe.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Because the Hebrew text of the final phrase is difficult, some scholars read it to mean that each man kept his weapon in his right hand.
